Investment memo · BALY-US · Viewforth

Bally's (BALY-US): a stable casino business inside a capital structure that consumes all of its earnings, which leaves the common equity a downward-skewed option on the sponsor, Chicago and the lenders

As at 4 November 2026. Share price $13.52 (2 November 2026); about 60.6m shares, including 11.62m penny warrants; market capitalisation about $0.85bn; FactSet enterprise value (EV) $6.8bn, including $1.5bn of minorities and lease-inclusive debt. All money is in US dollars unless marked in euros or sterling. Q3 2026 results (due about 10 November) are not yet in the figures. Definitions, the forecast basis and sources are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

The one-line case. Bally's is a stable, mildly growing casino and gaming business, earning about $730m of segment EBITDAR, inside a capital structure that consumes all of that EBITDAR, and its controlling sponsor lacks enough capital of its own to rescue it alone. Bally's common equity is therefore not a claim on gambling earnings. The common equity is an option on three outcomes: what the sponsor, Standard General, does by 31 March 2027; how fast the permanent Chicago casino ramps up from mid-2027; and whether the lenders and the landlord let the common equity survive the reset of the capital structure. Richard's framework looks for cases where fundamental outcomes and the probability of upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. Bally's is the mirror image: its operating forecasts are unusually predictable, and its equity outcome is unusually unpredictable and skewed down. That asymmetry is the most useful thing to know about Bally's, and it is knowable now.

Seven insights carry the case.

1
Bally's fixed charges exceed its earnings, both before and after the Chicago casino opens. On the model, segment EBITDAR covers rent plus interest 1.01x in FY2026, 0.86x in FY2027 and 0.89x in FY2028. Between FY2026 and FY2028, rent rises from $248m to $346m (the Chicago casino adds about $80m at opening) and reported interest rises from $477m to $592m. The parent company on its own (US casinos, US online and corporate) earns about $360m to $400m of EBITDAR against about $250m to $300m of rent and about $245m to $305m of cash interest, so the parent needs $300m to $400m of new funding a year even after Chicago stabilises. Operating improvements cannot close that gap; only a capital-structure event can.
2
The permanent Chicago casino reduces EBITDA in its first year. The casino's rent (8.5% a year on the $940m that the landlord, Gaming and Leisure Properties (GLPI), is funding) starts on opening day, while the casino's earnings ramp up over two to three years. In the base case, year one brings $65m of annualised EBITDAR against $80m of new rent and $13m of temporary-casino EBITDAR forgone, a net reduction of $28m. Consensus FY2027 EBITDA growth of +11.7% needs the Chicago casino to earn $150m to $250m annualised from its first quarter. Four pieces of evidence argue against that: the temporary casino runs at about a quarter of its target; video gaming terminals are already licensed at 78 Chicago sites; PENN has doubled its capacity at nearby Aurora; and the hotel has been cut from 500 rooms to about 100.
3
Consensus is too high on EBITDA and EPS, too low on interest, and about to be disguised by Evoke. FY2027 consensus EBITDA is $541m against our $459m (-15%); implied consensus interest is about $464m against our $582m (+$118m); consensus EPS is -$5.41 against our -$8.81. Three of the five broker estimates date from 17 August 2026, and none includes Evoke. The next wave of EBITDA and EPS revisions should therefore be downward. Revenue and headline EBITDA revisions will nonetheless turn positive in 2027, when Evoke is consolidated into the subsidiary, and that rise will be a false signal for the parent's equity.
4
Bally's best assets sit where the common equity cannot reach them. The UK online business (number two in UK online casino, marketing at only 11% of revenue, 65% of the duty increase mitigated, the best mitigation in the sector) and the lottery contracts sit inside Bally's Intralot, which Bally's owns 58% of and which is ring-fenced from the parent; the market value of that 58% stake (about $1.1bn to $1.4bn) exceeds Bally's whole market capitalisation. The Rhode Island monopoly to 2043 is real, but its payments to the parent are restricted while leverage is above 5.5x. The regional estate's property-level rent coverage (1.98x and 2.13x) protects GLPI, not Bally's shareholders.
5
Standard General is a backstop for Bally's solvency, not for the value held by minority shareholders. Standard General has $647m of discretionary assets under management (Form ADV, March 2026), and every large transaction it has done has used third-party capital (Apollo's 11% notes for the Queen merger; HPS at MediaCo). Standard General has bid for Bally's at $38, $15 and $18.25, and its Soo Kim is now Bally's Executive Chair. A rescue is plausible, but any rescue will be structured to rank senior to the common equity or to dilute it. The share price of $13.52, between the $8.44 capitulation low and the sponsor's $15 bid, shows the market treating the sponsor's past bid prices as the guide to a future one.
6
The next six months will deliver most of the information that decides the case. Q3 2026 results (about 10 November) will show liquidity against the $325m minimum and the revolving credit facility after its October step-down. Bally's Intralot's results on 27 November will show UK constant-currency growth after the cuts to player bonuses ("generosity") and whether the subsidiary's €422m EBITDA guidance survives. The Chicago host-agreement deadline falls on 10 December. The FY2026 10-K and the refinancing are due by 31 March 2027. Each of these events is dated and observable, and most are negative in expectation.
7
Two events together would turn Bally's into a setup Richard wants. The first is a completed recapitalisation that removes the going-concern doubt at a blended cost below 10%. The second is Illinois Gaming Board receipts for the permanent Chicago casino above about $30m a month in its first quarters. Together, the two events would convert the case from a solvency option into a "Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU" setup (one of Viewforth's Target Setups) with real scope for EBITDA upgrades, because consensus would then be too low on Chicago and too high on interest. I put a 5% to 10% probability on that combination within 18 months; the calendar in #10 names the data releases that would reveal it.

Five judgements move the value of the shares most over one to two years. Each $10m of EBITDA after rent is worth about $0.16 a share on about 61m shares, and because the equity is about eight times geared to enterprise value, a 10% change in EV moves equity value by roughly 80%.

Counterparties, not Bally's, set judgements 1 and 2. Judgement 3, the Chicago ramp-up, is the only large upside, and it is binary. Judgements 4 and 5 are the ordinary operating arguments, and they move the value least.

Implication for the decision: time works against the common equity unless an event intervenes. On the model's own base case, net debt rises about $0.66bn in FY2027 and $0.53bn in FY2028 while EBITDA after rent stays flat, so the equity's value erodes every year. The upside tail is real, because a sponsor bid or a clean refinancing would re-rate a thin free float sharply, but that tail carries only a 5% to 10% probability. The downside cluster (a sponsor-led recapitalisation on dilutive terms, or a restructuring) carries 50%. An investor who wants exposure to the parts of the Bally's story that work has cleaner instruments: the listed subsidiary, Bally's Intralot (BYLOT-GR), for UK consolidation, and the landlord, GLPI, for the property economics. The parent's common equity is the residual claim behind both.

1#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Conclusion: the operating environment is stable on demand and hostile on every price Bally's pays for capital, real estate and tax, so it offers no tailwind that reaches the common equity.

EvidenceCustomer demand is holding. US regional gross gaming revenue grew +3.5% in Q2 and +3.6% in Q3 2026, though growth slowed to +2.5% in September, and Morgan Stanley forecasts it flat in 2027. At Bally's, rated visitation (play by customers tracked in the loyalty programme) rose 4.3% in Q2, while unrated and lower-tier play fell. UK online gaming grew 10.5%, 11.6% and about 13% in constant currency in Q1, Q2 and July 2026, and the scaled UK peers reported +12% to +14% growth in Q3. Bally's North America Interactive grew 16.9% in Q2 while its industry slowed from 16% to 13% growth.

EvidenceThree external forces are moving, and all three move against the parent company. First, Bally's cost of capital has risen to 11% to 13%: its unsecured notes trade at 63% to 70% of par, euro high-yield spreads have widened 90bp since September, and the market is in a credit-led risk-off regime (the dashboard's "Fragility Double Underweight"). Second, fiscal policy has tightened: UK Remote Gaming Duty rose from 21% to 40% in April 2026 and UK Betting Duty rises from 15% to 25% in April 2027, together a gross cost of about €120m a year at the subsidiary, while Chicago's online betting tax rose from 2% to 10.25%. Third, municipal politics have turned: Chicago legalised video gaming terminals in August 2026, the state had licensed 78 Chicago sites by late October, and the terminal operator Accel received its first city permits on 3 November 2026.

Inference: the industry is sound, but the external change transfers value away from Bally's. The industry's structure suits a well-capitalised incumbent: licence-capped local oligopolies with rational, return-focused competitors (Boyd at 2.5x leverage, Red Rock returning cash, PENN relocating casinos rather than cutting prices). The external change moves value along the chain to landlords (8.5% yields with annual rent escalators), to lenders and to tax authorities. Where the industry does have a tailwind, in tax-driven UK consolidation toward scale, Bally's holds that tailwind only through its 58%-owned subsidiary.

So what for the forecasts. Model 2027 core regional revenue at 0% to +2% with a downside skew, hard-code the UK duty steps, and assume no regulatory relief anywhere. The one positive external force, UK consolidation, is already in the forecast recovery of the UK online (B2C, business-to-consumer) margin to 29% to 30%, and it does not reach the parent's fixed-charge line.

Strongest counter-case: the consumer is resilient. The regional consumer has been more resilient than sentiment suggests (Boyd saw "no material impact" from fuel prices). UK growth after the duty increase has been stronger than any peer feared, and Machine Games Duty was set at 25% rather than the feared 40%, a clearing event for the sector. If the demand base holds, the operating model is not the risk. I agree, and that is the point: the environment is benign enough for a creditor and irrelevant to the equity.

What would change my view. Any of three developments would: a settlement of Chicago's video-terminal dispute that caps terminals near the casino; passage of the Class 7b property-tax incentive, worth about $13m a year; or a 150bp fall in Bally's marginal cost of debt.

Market versus me: the market blames the sector, but the data point to Bally's balance sheet. The market narrative treats the sector de-rating (Flutter -62% and Entain -39% over twelve months) as Bally's problem, yet the peer basket explains only 1% of the daily variance in Bally's share price. The market also under-weights the rollout of video terminals in Chicago, which is now live, and over-weights the risk to the consumer.

Score: 21, set by the Rater. Demand is not the problem (US regional gaming revenue +2.5% to +3.6%, UK online +10% to +13%), but every enacted or live external force on the business moves against it: UK Remote Gaming Duty 21% to 40% and Betting Duty to 25% (about EUR 120m gross at the subsidiary), Chicago's video gaming terminals now licensed at 78 sites diluting the flagship's exclusivity, PENN's doubled Aurora capacity, and credit markets pricing Bally's at 11% to 13%; the one tailwind, UK consolidation, sits in a 58%-owned ring-fenced subsidiary and is already in its margin recovery. No figure in figures.md measures this directly; coherent with the External change forces group at 20, I place it just below BP (a structural drag on the main earnings line) and above Yara, because demand itself holds.

2#2 Internally-driven corporate change

Conclusion: internal change at Bally's is extensive but mostly defensive or value-transferring, and the change that matters most, a sponsor-led capital-structure event, is likelier to crystallise losses for minority shareholders than to cure them.

EvidenceThe real positives are operational. North America Interactive moved from a $40m segment loss in FY2024 to +$3.0m of EBITDAR in Q2 2026 by moving onto variable-cost platforms. The landside conversions at Baton Rouge and Marquette (moving gaming from riverboats onto land) worked: Baton Rouge gaming revenue rose about 590%. Bally's Intralot offset 65% of the Q2 duty hit (€11.3m from cost savings and €10.1m from growth), and it has €41m of merger synergies and a €50m mitigation plan in hand. The permanent Chicago casino's structure topped off in July 2026, with GLPI having funded $640.7m of its $940m commitment.

EvidenceThe real negatives are in control, finance and capital allocation. Control is centralised in Standard General: Soo Kim has been Executive Chair since January 2026, the sponsor owns 66.8% of the shares, and the board has no lead independent director. The finance function has been hollowed out: there have been three CFO changes since May 2023; the treasurer left in April 2026 and has not been replaced; the President doubles as interim CFO; and the CEO is also Group CEO of Bally's Intralot. Disclosure controls are ineffective, tax accounting has a material weakness, and two filings were late in 2026. Finally, Bally's actions contradict its stated pivot to capital preservation (Q2 10-Q): it bought Sam's Town in August 2026, bought $42.7m of Bally's Intralot shares in H1, paid $500m for the Bronx licence and $115m for a golf concession in Q1, and Soo Kim added Star shares in October.

Inference: the operational change is small, and the structural change points to a capital event priced for the capital provider. The operational improvements are worth tens of millions of dollars a year by 2027, arrive late, and about half of the online improvement is shared with Bally's Intralot once the online business passes breakeven. The decisive change is structural. Concentrated control and the loss of the finance team together make a sponsor-led capital-structure event the most likely next step. Every financing since 2024 has cost more than the one before (sale-leasebacks at 8% to 8.5%, then 11% notes, then loans at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) plus 750bp and plus 850bp), which says the next financing will also be priced for the capital provider.

So what: model the internal improvements as small, and watch the CFO appointment. The internal improvements should be modelled as small, back-ended and partly leaking to minority shareholders. The permanent CFO appointment is the clearest signal of the route the sponsor intends: a capital-markets banker would signal a refinancing; a restructuring specialist (as the former CFO, Mircheva, was) would signal a debt exchange.

Strongest counter-case: this management and this sponsor have created value before. The CEO, Reeves, built Gamesys from £340m to £709m of revenue and cut its leverage from 3.8x to 1.1x. The Intralot combination (at about 8.5x forward EBITDA, with €1.53bn of cash to Bally's) genuinely crystallised value. Standard General has repeatedly put capital in, and a sponsor with 67% of the equity and executive control has every incentive to find a solution. All true, and a solution will be found; the question is on whose terms. The precedents (Station Casinos in 2009 and Caesars' operating company in 2015) show sponsors keeping the assets while public equity holders bore the losses.

What would change my view. Any of three events would: an equity injection by Standard General at or above the market price with no senior instrument attached; a permanent CFO from a capital-markets background; or disclosure of a parent-only statement of sources and uses of cash.

Market versus me: the market reads new money as safety; I read it as more fixed charges. The market reads the WhiteHawk loan and GLPI's continued funding of Chicago as "liquidity ensured", and the shares rallied 60% from their low on those headlines. I read both as additional fixed charges that worsen the arithmetic. The market also still treats Standard General as good for a $500m cheque; Standard General's own capital of $647m says otherwise.

Score: 10, set by the Rater. The real operating positives (North America Interactive at breakeven, the Baton Rouge and Marquette conversions, the subsidiary's 65% duty mitigation, the Chicago structure topped off) are worth tens of millions, are back-ended and half leak to minorities, while control is concentrated in the sponsor as Executive Chair, the finance function is hollowed out (three CFO changes, no treasurer, a material weakness, two late filings) and debt-funded deals (Sam's Town, the USD 500m Bronx licence) contradict the stated capital preservation; the decisive change is a sponsor-led capital-structure event likelier to crystallise minority losses than to cure them. A self-inflicted repair on dilutive terms is the 10 level; coherent with the group's 14, I place it between TT Electronics (leadership churn and a restatement, with some recovery) and Alfen (covenant breached, targets withdrawn), nearer Alfen because a going-concern note now sits on top.

3#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Conclusion: Bally's operates in a sound industry for well-capitalised operators, but it holds a weak position in its value chain, has the sector's worst financial profile and runs a governance structure that puts the controlling shareholder first; the moats it has are owned 58% or restricted.

Value chain: Bally's sits in the squeezed middle of a chain that rewards the capacity to reinvest. Landlords earn EBITDA margins above 80% and 8.5% yields; the three largest slot-machine makers hold about 75% of casino floors and raise lease prices 3% to 5% a year; lenders price Bally's debt at 11% to 13%; and tax authorities treat gaming as a source of revenue. Bally's earns EBITDAR margins in the mid-to-high 20s (Casinos & Resorts 27.3% in Q2 2026, against a regional peer average in the mid-30s and about 47% at Boyd's locals casinos), and those margins shrink to the low single digits after rent, depreciation and amortisation, and interest.

Bally's under-invests in its casinos to service its debt. Maintenance capital expenditure runs at about 4.4% of casino revenue against an industry norm of 6% to 8%, and Deutsche Bank says Bally's leverage "prevents [it] from investing in legacy property maintenance to defend market share". The effects are already visible: Bally's Missouri market share fell 30bp in August 2026, and its Atlantic City business keeps shrinking.

Competitive advantage: the parent owns only one strong moat outright. Rhode Island, where Bally's runs both casinos and the only online casino under rights to 2043, is a strong and durable moat. Chicago's downtown exclusivity is valuable but is being diluted by video gaming terminals before the casino opens. The UK online business (data-led, bingo-led and low on marketing, with a 43% standalone margin before the duty) is a strong moat, and the lottery contracts' switching costs are a moderate one, but Bally's owns only 58% of both. US online has no moat: Bally's holds about 2% of the Pennsylvania market, and industry experts call it "significantly behind" with "no differentiation".

Financial profile: Bally's is among the weakest in the listed European and US gaming cohort. Net debt is 18x EBITDA on FactSet's lease-inclusive basis (Entain 3.1x, Evoke 5.1x, Betsson net cash), and rent-adjusted leverage at the parent is 13x to 16x (Deutsche Bank: 14.0x pro forma). Return on invested capital was negative (-2.9% in FY2024), with over $770m of impairments in eighteen months. The EBIT margin was 1.1% in FY2025. Free cash flow has been negative every year since FY2021; consensus has -$480m for FY2026 and our model has -$1,025m, including the New York licence. Tangible book equity is already negative: intangible assets of $2.86bn exceed the $2.35bn of equity attributable to shareholders.

Bally's reported earnings overstate its underlying profit. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $124m while the net loss was $164m; "one-off" charges recur at $40m to $110m a year; and a $105.8m gain on a sale-leaseback flattered Q1 2026.

Management: a capable operator CEO under a controlling shareholder who sets an expansive strategy. The CEO is a capable digital operator who fixed North America Interactive and built the UK franchise. The strategy, however, is set by the controlling shareholder, who is pursuing more than $5bn of developments (Chicago, the Bronx, Las Vegas, Star, Evoke) while returns on capital are negative.

Management's record is one of cuts, misses and delays. Guidance was cut twice in 2022 and again in 2023, set below consensus in 2024, and has been abandoned since; every quarter of 2024 missed on EBITDAR. The temporary Chicago casino opened months late, and the permanent casino's opening has slipped from "late 2026" to "spring 2027". Pay is discretionary: the 2023 target of $557m of EBITDA was abandoned, yet 100% of the performance share units paid out. The Leadership digest puts Bally's in the bottom percentile on pay for performance.

Inference and so what: the advantages are real but sit in the wrong places. Do not model margin expansion at the parent from competitive advantage. Model Rhode Island as a floor; model Chicago with a haircut for the video terminals (stabilised revenue of $500m against Deutsche Bank's $703m); and model UK market-share gains at a 58% look-through.

Strongest counter-case: the regional estate is a good business with a motivated landlord. Property-level rent coverage of 1.98x and 2.13x is above Caesars' regional lease (about 1.6x) and PENN's Pinnacle lease (1.70x). GLPI, which draws 19.4% of its cash income from Bally's, has every incentive to keep its tenant whole. Both points are true, and both are arguments for owning the credit and the landlord rather than the common equity.

What would change my view. Any of three developments would: maintenance capital expenditure rising toward 6% of casino revenue; a Chicago settlement that restores the casino's exclusivity; or a finance team that stays stable through a refinancing.

Market versus me: the sell-side understates Bally's leverage by about $370m of EBITDA a year. The sell-side's stated reason for its Hold ratings is leverage, not operations. I agree on operations, but I think the brokers understate the leverage, because the ring-fence around Bally's Intralot means consolidated EBITDA overstates the earnings available to service parent debt by about $370m a year. The chart below shows the parent's own position, and the diagram after it shows how the ring-fence divides the group.

Score: 13, set by the Rater. Qualitatively the industry is sound (licence-capped local oligopolies, rational rivals) and Rhode Island is a real moat to 2043, but Bally's sits in the squeezed middle of its chain (landlord, lenders, slot makers and fiscal authorities take the value), Chicago's moat is being diluted before it opens, the UK and lottery moats are 58% owned, US online has none, maintenance capex runs at 4.4% of casino revenue against a 6% to 8% norm and the management serves the controlling holder (guidance abandoned, pay discretionary). The figures tell the truth and are worse than BP's: ROIC -11.5% (2nd percentile), operating margin 1.1% (6th), net debt to EBITDA 16.1x (99th, worst), free cash flow negative since FY2021, and the new capital (Chicago, the Bronx) is forecast to earn below its 8.5% to 13% cost for years; coherent with the groups (30, 27, 4, 9), I place it below BP and above SMA, which lacks even Bally's local protections.

4#4 Guidance, expectations management and track record

Conclusion: Bally's has no guidance that could prove conservative, its subsidiary's guidance is above the run-rate, and the group's record is one of cuts and abandonment, so this topic contributes nothing to a positive skew.

The parent gives no guidance, and the only live guidance in the group sits above its run-rate. Bally's gives no consolidated guidance for FY2026 or FY2027 and has given none since FY2024, when it delivered at the low end of its range. The only quantified guidance in the group is Bally's Intralot's: FY2026 adjusted EBITDA of about €422m (reaffirmed in May 2026) and a pro forma FY2027 target of €454m. H1 2026 EBITDA was €184.8m, so €422m needs a second half of about €237m, 28% above the first. The CEO's own outlook for Interactive (€280m to €295m) plus the lottery run-rate (about €104m) sums to only €384m to €399m. In FY2025 the subsidiary delivered €430.8m against a €435m target.

Management's informal commentary is more optimistic than its formal disclosures. Statements such as "development liquidity ensured", Chicago "on track" and "transformative", and "strong revenue tailwinds" appeared in the same quarter as a going-concern note and the statement that the company "does not project meeting liquidity maintenance... without additional financing".

Inference: there is no conservatism to unwind, and the subsidiary's guidance is likely to be cut. Bally's has no record of raising guidance. I put about 60% on Bally's Intralot's €422m being rebased to the high €390s or low €400s, either on 27 November or with the FY2026 results. The rebase would probably be presented alongside Evoke's completion, with a combined outlook that lets the €454m target be retired without a visible cut. Management's informal milestones will fall into three groups: met (North America Interactive profitable), missed (the permanent Chicago casino opening by 30 June 2027) and met-then-missed ("development liquidity ensured" holds only until the WhiteHawk loan matures in April 2028).

So what: build forecasts from drivers and dated events, not from company statements. The primary sources should be GLPI's filings, the separate 10-Q of Bally's Chicago, Inc. and Bally's Intralot's reports in Athens. A rebase of the subsidiary's guidance is worth only about $14m of consolidated EBITDAR and $0.13 a share after minorities. Its signal is larger than its size: it would be the first cut to any number in the group since 2023, and it would land in the middle of the parent's refinancing negotiation.

Strongest counter-case: the subsidiary's building blocks are specific and its management has delivered before. The plan names €25m from lower player bonuses, €10m from costs and €15m from synergies, plus £180m of Evoke synergies by year two at a £25m cost to achieve. Evoke's management delivered £150m of synergies against a £100m target on William Hill, and the UK peers' Q3 results argue that €422m could be held with a small miss (30%). That is fair, but it changes the size of the signal, not its direction.

What would change my view. Either of two events would: Bally's reinstating guidance after a signed refinancing, which would show that the lenders' terms are settled; or Bally's Intralot reporting Q3 UK constant-currency growth at or above 6% while keeping €422m.

Market versus me: the absence of guidance reflects the going-concern position, not the take-private. The market treats the absence of guidance as a legacy of the 2025 take-private. I think it reflects the going-concern position, and guidance will not return before the capital structure is settled; I put about 20% on any guidance within 18 months.

Score: 9, set by the Rater. Guidance was cut twice in 2022 and again in 2023, delivered only at the low end in 2024 and abandoned since; every quarter of 2024 missed EBITDAR, the permanent Chicago casino slipped from late 2026 to spring 2027, and the only live guidance (the subsidiary's EUR 422m) needs an H2 28% above H1 against the CEO's own building blocks summing to EUR 384m to 399m, so current guidance sits above what can be delivered while informal claims ('liquidity ensured') sat beside a going-concern note. The absence of parent guidance is not itself negative, but the record is the 10 level of serial cuts and abandonment; coherent with the Guidance group's 13 and the Sell-side group's 20, I place it below Judges Scientific's warnings and above Wizz Air's suspension and collapse.

5#5 Business model: pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out, feedback loops

Conclusion: Bally's business model has extreme leverage pointed the wrong way, no pricing power at the parent and no cuttable cost that matters, so revenue growth produces outsized losses until a capital-structure event changes the fixed charges.

Pricing power: Bally's has shown it only by passing UK tax on to players. The €25m cut to player bonuses is a price rise that recovers about a fifth of the margin lost to the duty, and the players' response stays untested until Bally's Intralot reports on 27 November. Rhode Island has no price lever, because the state sets the economics. US online is a price-taker. The Chicago casino will need negative pricing (promotions at 12% to 13.5% of gaming revenue) to build its customer database. In total, pricing adds about +$20m of EBITDA in FY2027 and nothing after.

Operating leverage: high, and about to rise further. Casinos & Resorts converts about 55% of incremental revenue into EBITDAR. North America Interactive's cost base is now variable, with incremental margins of 15% to 25%. In UK online, the incremental margin fell from about 50% to about 30% because 40% of each pound of gaming revenue now goes to tax. Meanwhile, fixed charges (rent plus interest) rose from about $140m in FY2021 to $430m in FY2024, and the model has them at $725m in FY2026 and $884m in FY2027, while EBITDAR only roughly doubled. The Chicago casino adds $80m of fixed rent from opening into a business with a 20% margin in its first year. Operating leverage therefore works against every line below revenue until FY2029.

Financial leverage: the defining feature of the business model. The equity is about eight times geared to enterprise value. Each 100bp on the interest rate of about $3bn of parent debt costs $30m a year, or $0.49 a share. Each $100m of deficit funded with debt at 13% adds $13m of interest, or $0.21 a share, the following year.

Cash interest is lower than reported interest, which helps the credit. Reported interest includes about $85m a year of non-cash accretion on the 2029 and 2031 notes until 2029, so the parent's cash interest is about $230m to $245m in FY2026. Nobody on the sell-side has articulated this point.

Cost-out: real but small, and the costs that matter cannot be cut. Cost programmes add about $30m to $45m of EBITDA in FY2027 and $60m to $80m of run-rate savings by FY2028, mostly at the subsidiary (58% ours) and already inside the forecast segment margins. The parent's own pool of cuttable cost is $30m to $60m. The costs that matter, rent and interest, cannot be cut outside a restructuring: GLPI collected 100% of its rent through the 2020 closures and has never forgiven rent, and Caesars' operating company cut its interest by 75% only through Chapter 11.

Feedback loops: the dominant loop is financial and negative. A $300m to $400m parent deficit funded at 12% to 13% adds $40m to $60m of interest a year, so the loss per share does not converge. Four slower loops sit alongside it. Under-investment takes 0.5 to 1 point a year off core revenue. The Chicago loop is balancing until FY2029, because the rent arrives before the earnings. UK consolidation is a positive, reinforcing loop, but offshore leakage caps it: the UK's unlicensed offshore market has tripled to £685m of gaming yield since 2019, and the Dutch market shrank about 25% after its tax rose to 34.2%. Finally, the interests of GLPI and Standard General are balancing loops that keep the company alive without improving it.

So what: in the base case, revenue growth leads to smaller profits through FY2028. Bally's leverage is the opposite of what Richard's framework wants, because it converts a flat operating base into a widening loss and a shrinking equity claim.

Strongest counter-case: the leverage cuts both ways. If the Chicago casino ramps up at Deutsche Bank's $160m to $250m, the same gearing turns a $95m EBITDA beat into $0.6bn of enterprise value, 70% of today's market capitalisation. That is the bull case, and it is honest; but it rests on one binary driver.

What would change my view. Either of two developments would. The first is an interest line that falls: an exchange of the unsecured notes at the market's 63% to 70% of par could cut their face value by up to about $450m and be neutral or positive for the equity. The second is evidence that property-level rent coverage lets GLPI concede relief on capital expenditure, as VICI did for Caesars in 2020.

Market versus me: only one credit desk has articulated the parent's own gap. The sell-side models consolidated leverage, and only Deutsche Bank's credit desk has articulated the parent's own funding gap. The market has not priced the fact that the Chicago casino's opening lowers FY2027 EBITDA.

Score: 15, set by the Rater. The structure has real operating gearing at property level (Casinos & Resorts flow-through about 55%) and extreme financial gearing (equity about eight times geared to EV), but the gears point the wrong way: fixed charges rise from USD 725m to 884m in FY2027 while EBITDAR barely moves, Chicago's USD 80m rent lands before its earnings, B2C's incremental margin fell from about 50% to 30% under the duty, there is no pricing power at the parent, the cuttable pool is USD 30m to 60m, and the dominant loop is a debt-funded deficit adding USD 40m to 60m of interest a year so that revenue growth gives wider losses through FY2028. The forecast ratio is meaningless (losses throughout); this is close to the 10 level (leverage stretched and running in reverse, no cost-out that matters), held a little above it because the same gearing would amplify a strong Chicago ramp and USD 85m a year of the interest is non-cash accretion.

6#6 Forecast financials: growth and margins over the next four years

Conclusion: revenue grows at mid-single digits, but fixed charges grow faster, so losses widen and equity shrinks through the forecast period; there is no double-digit earnings growth to find.

The forecasts of record (model update 1): revenue grows every year, but net interest outgrows EBITDA after rent.

Revenue growth comes from consolidation and from Chicago, not from the core estate. Consolidation adds a full year of Intralot's lottery business and Bilyoner in FY2026, and Sam's Town from August 2026. Chicago's revenue rises from $150m at the temporary casino to $238m, $375m, $450m and $488m. The core casino estate is flat in FY2027 and grows only 0.5% to 1% a year after that.

The margin after rent troughs in FY2027 to FY2028 and never regains its FY2025 level. The EBITDA-after-rent margin falls to 13.8% to 13.9% in FY2027 to FY2028, from 20% in FY2024, because rent rises by about $100m and the UK duty permanently removes 7 to 8 points of UK online margin. The margin recovers only to 15.4% by FY2030, still below FY2025.

Chicago's extra rent cancels every operating gain between FY2026 and FY2028. EBITDA after rent moves from $483m to $486m. Chicago's EBITDAR adds $75m, North America Interactive $16m, UK online $15m and Sam's Town $9m, while the core casinos subtract $6m, the lottery business (B2B, business-to-business) $10m and rent $98m. Chicago's earnings gain is smaller than its rent through FY2028, and everything else nets to about +$9m.

There is no scope for double-digit earnings growth. EBITDA after rent grows 6% in FY2028 and 13% in FY2029, the first year in which Chicago's EBITDAR overtakes its rent, but interest grows faster, so the adjusted loss stays flat at about -$8.6 to -$8.9 a share from FY2027. Attributable book equity falls from about $2.1bn to about zero by 2030. On the Analyst's cross-check, free cash flow is negative in every year even excluding the Bronx: about -$480m in FY2027 and -$300m to -$320m a year after that.

Growth and margins will be lower than in the past, not higher. The FY2026 to FY2030 EBITDAR margin of 23% to 25% is below FY2025's inferred 26%. Net interest at 15% to 17% of revenue is about nine times the 1.85% of the FfF comparison sample.

Our base case already leans below consensus, and the remaining skew is still down on cash and EPS. The base case has the Chicago casino opening a quarter late and reaching 60% of the analysts' stabilised figure, the core casinos flat, UK online below consensus and interest well above consensus. After that lean, the remaining skew is down on cash and EPS and two-sided on EBITDA: for FY2027, bear $380m, base $459m and bull $560m to $610m. The bull case rests on Chicago alone.

Evoke will make reported growth jump without changing the equity case. Evoke is not in the base case. Its completion, expected around Q1 to Q2 2027, adds about $1.75bn of revenue and $250m of EBITDA for nine months of FY2027 (about $2.35bn and $420m in FY2028) and about $2.4bn of ring-fenced debt. In an all-share outcome it dilutes Bally's stake in Bally's Intralot toward 51%, and it changes Bally's EPS by about nil.

Strongest counter-case: consensus sees EBITDA rising to $630m and free cash flow turning positive. Consensus EBITDA is $541m for FY2027 and $630m for FY2028, with free cash flow of +$44m in FY2028. That path needs three things: the Chicago casino accretive after rent from its first quarter, interest flat despite the WhiteHawk loan and the repricing of existing debt, and no spending on the Bronx. Each assumption is more likely to be cut than confirmed.

What would change my view. Any of three outcomes would: an Illinois Gaming Board monthly figure above $30m for the Chicago casino in its first full quarter; UK online growth holding at +6% through the bonus cuts; or a refinancing below 10%.

Market versus me: consensus misses rent at opening and the repricing of debt. For FY2027 we are 4% below consensus on revenue, 15% below on EBITDA, $118m above on interest and $3.40 a share worse on EPS. The two reasons are the rent that starts when Chicago opens and the repricing of Bally's debt, and consensus models neither.

Score: 5, set by the Rater. The measure gives F, and I place it near the floor of the band: the margin after rent troughs at 13.8% to 13.9% and recovers only to 15.4% by FY2030, below FY2024's 20% and FY2025's 19%, net interest grows faster than EBITDA, and the mid-single-digit revenue growth is mostly bought or consolidated (Intralot, Sam's Town) plus a Chicago ramp whose rent outruns its earnings until FY2029. It is the 10 level (earnings falling with no route back and margins below the past), with free cash flow negative every year and book equity heading to zero; the Financial forecasts group at 4 agrees.

7#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: over the next 6 to 12 months the scope is for cuts to EBITDA and EPS estimates and mechanical rises in revenue estimates; the only genuine upgrade window is a strong Chicago opening in mid-2027.

Brokers have cut below the operating line and have not yet touched EBITDA. Since August, FY2027 consensus EPS has fallen 24% over three months while revenue is unchanged and EBITDA is down 9%. The gaps between consensus and our base (EBITDA 15% lower, interest $118m higher) sit exactly where the next cuts will fall, and dated events will force them. The Q3 2026 results will reprice interest for the WhiteHawk loan. The FY2026 10-K and the refinancing (March 2027) will reprice the whole interest line. The Q1 and Q2 2027 results will put the Chicago casino's rent and ramp-up into the models as actuals. FY2028 estimates, which only two brokers publish for EBITDA, are the most exposed. My probabilities for each revision are in the figure below.

There is one earnings-driven upgrade window, and it depends on Chicago. If the Chicago casino opens strongly, Q2 to Q3 2027 is the window in which EBITDA consensus could rise (about 20%). The other routes to upgrades are not driven by earnings: a capital-structure event that removes the going-concern doubt would probably bring one or two moves from Hold to Buy on "survival", and a sponsor bid would move ratings to the bid price.

The perimeter trap: Evoke will make revisions look positive when they are not. When Evoke completes, consolidated revenue rises about 55% and headline EBITDA about 50%, so the dashboard's revision statistics for sales and EBITDA will turn strongly positive for reasons unrelated to the parent's claim. Judge revisions on EBITDA after rent and after minorities, or per share.

Inference and so what: the configuration Richard wants is absent on every line the share price trades on. Richard's framework wants estimates below what the forecasts will deliver. The only expectations below our forecasts are FY2026 free cash flow and some brokers' EPS bases, and neither moves the stock.

Strongest counter-case: expectations are so bleak that any survival re-rates the stock. No broker rates Bally's a Buy, and the mean target of $10.50 is 22% below the price. The 60% rally from $8.44 on a 13% bridge loan showed how far survival news can move the shares. That is true, and it is the honest bull case, but it is a trade on a financing headline against the sponsor's incentives, not an upgrade cycle.

What would change my view. Either of two events would: disclosure on the Q3 call of the timing of Chicago's rent that shows consensus already carries it (unlikely, because nobody has asked); or the Chicago casino opening in April 2027 with receipts similar to Deutsche Bank's forecast.

Market versus me: the equity narrative has absorbed none of the parent-level mechanics. The equity narrative carries management's Chicago figure of $250m; ours is $150m. The narrative has not absorbed the parent's own cash gap, the timing of rent before earnings, the sponsor's limited capital or the covenant mechanics. One credit desk and the landlord's filings set these points out; nobody on the equity side does.

Score: 8, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most: the subsidiary's EUR 422m is about 60% likely to be rebased, the first cut in the group since 2023, and the parent has none to raise. Consensus: FY2027 EBITDA is about 15% above the model and EPS about USD 3.40 worse on the model (-8.81 against -5.41) because interest is USD 118m too low, with about 70% odds of a 10% EBITDA cut and 75% of further EPS cuts; against about 6% revenue growth that is a negative ratio of two or more, below the Universe's bottom decile, and the coming Evoke perimeter jump in revenue is not an upgrade. The narrative's only upside is a financing headline or a strong Chicago opening (about 20%), so with the fourth set group at 11 I place it just above Fugro (withdrawn guidance, further cuts) and below Entra.

8#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: momentum is negative in guidance, estimates and narrative, neutral-to-recovering in the technicals on a thin free float, and negative across the sector, with no fundamental driver of upgrades in sight.

Sell-side momentum is negative and stale. All five covering brokers rate the shares Hold or Sell. FY2027 consensus EPS has fallen 24% over three months and 140% over twelve; the mean target price has fallen 14% over three months; the dashboard's revision-momentum score is -8; and three of the five estimates date from 17 August. Breadth cannot fall further in the ordinary sense, so the realistic next change is coverage attrition: Deutsche Bank and Jefferies have already dropped equity coverage.

Narrative momentum is negative for both the sector and the company. The sector narrative is negative because of prediction markets, the UK duty and the de-rating of Flutter and Entain. Bally's own narrative is separately negative: the going-concern note on 14 August, the CFO's exit on 3 September and GLPI's public warning on 29 October. The share price recovered on a financing headline, not on a change in the facts.

Technical momentum is recovering, but on a thin free float and on headlines. The dashboard rates technical momentum D. The price of $13.52 is above the 50-day ($12.01), 150-day ($12.58) and 200-day ($12.91) moving averages, and the 200-day average has risen in nine of the last twelve months. Relative strength is in the 25th percentile, the shares are down 27.4% over twelve months, and the 52-week range is $8.44 to $19.60. The free float is thin (about 20m shares, trading about 120,000 shares or $1.3m a day) and is building a base after capitulation. Because peers explain only 1% of the share price's variance, the price moves in gaps on headlines rather than in a drift.

Peers' ratings are weak, but their operating news is better than their ratings. Sector thematic momentum is F across all 13 names on the dashboard. On technical momentum, Evolution, Evoke and Lottomatica rate B, Bally's Intralot D, and Flutter and Entain F. On sell-side momentum, Betsson rates B and most others D or F. The operating read-across is better: PENN raised its retail guidance twice in 2026 and was upgraded on deleveraging, Boyd was upgraded in October, and UK online peers reported double-digit growth in Q3. Regional and UK demand are holding; the sector de-rating is about tax, prediction markets and, for Bally's alone, solvency.

Inference and so what: nothing in Bally's momentum supports entry. There is no momentum in guidance or estimates, and none in prospect from the fundamentals. The technical bounce is an event driven by a liquidity headline in a thin free float, and a momentum-led framework should not treat it as a signal to buy.

Strongest counter-case: the technical indicators are improving, and thin stocks move fast. The price is above all its moving averages, the 200-day average is rising, and in a stock this thin a change in the narrative moves the price far and fast. That is true in both directions: the shares fell 26% on one sentence in a 10-Q.

What would change my view. Either of two events would: two consecutive clean quarters with the going-concern language removed; or a Buy initiation built on a parent-level model.

Market versus me: the dashboard reads a turn; I read a relief rally. The dashboard's rule reads the technical indicators as "Turning/Inflecting". I read them as a relief rally on a bridge loan. The next headlines (Q3 liquidity, Bally's Intralot on 27 November and the Chicago deadline on 10 December) will decide which reading is right.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. Both measures negative gives D, and the parts confirm the low end: no parent guidance and the subsidiary's at risk, consensus EPS -24% over three and -26% over six months (3rd and 5th percentiles), 0% Buy, targets -14%, a distressed narrative, and sector peers F on thematic momentum. Only the technicals hold it off F: the price is above its 50, 150 and 200-day averages with the 200-day rising after the USD 8.44 capitulation, though that is a headline-driven bounce in a thin float, so I place it near the floor of D.

9#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: the operating forecast is simple and trackable, but the equity forecast is a binary outcome set by counterparties within six months, with risks that are sudden, high-magnitude, correlated and now part of the base case rather than the tail.

The case is unusually simple above the fixed-charge line and unusually complex below it. Four drivers explain nearly all of the change from FY2025 to FY2028: the rent steps, the interest bill, the UK duty and the Chicago casino's ramp-up. Only the Chicago ramp-up has a wide range. The ordinary operating arguments (demand, pricing, cost programmes and North America Interactive) move EBITDA by only about $25m either way over the whole period. The equity case is therefore a two-variable problem, Chicago and the financing, with the UK as a third.

Our base case needs three things; consensus needs three things Bally's has never shown. Our base case needs a debt bridge to be available at about 13% at all, the Chicago casino to reach $150m of stabilised EBITDAR by FY2030 (the temporary casino's $13m is no guide), and the UK base to hold through the bonus cuts. Consensus needs three strengths Bally's has not demonstrated: on-time delivery of a $1.7bn urban project, an urban ramp-up faster than peers achieved, and a refinancing on better terms than the last one. Management capacity is the fragility beneath all of these requirements: Bally's has had four finance heads in under four years, and it faces a refinancing, the Chicago opening, the Evoke integration and the Bronx project at the same time.

The high-magnitude risks are no longer low-probability: a covenant or liquidity event is the base-case risk, not a tail. The table below sets out the dated mechanisms. Three details matter beyond the table. The first-lien leverage test cannot be met through operations in May 2027 on any plausible EBITDA, but it applies only when revolver use exceeds 25% of commitments, and equity can cure it twice in four quarters. The AlphaSense report also cites a July 2026 extension of $460m of revolver commitments to October 2028, which conflicts with the $319m after the step-down and which the Q3 10-Q must reconcile. And if the 2029 notes are not refinanced, the term loan's maturity springs forward to 1 March 2029, which forces the question of the unsecured notes into 2028.

Further risks sit outside the debt documents, and they reinforce one another. In Chicago, the temporary casino's licence runs only to 25 October 2027, and the video terminals keep spreading. Bally's internal controls carry restatement risk; a reported SEC inquiry comes from a weak source and is unverified. Bally's stake in Star carries an A$260m penalty and mark-to-market noise. Sterling matters: a 10% move changes UK online EBITDAR by about $29m. These risks reinforce rather than offset each other: a weak Chicago ramp-up worsens the financing loop and the political loop at once.

The case is more trackable than the company's disclosure suggests, except for the thing that matters most. Third parties publish on their own calendars: GLPI quarterly (funding, rent coverage, warnings), Bally's Chicago, Inc. in its own 10-Q, the Illinois Gaming Board monthly by casino, the states monthly on gaming revenue, Bally's Intralot quarterly in Athens, and the bond market daily. The blind spot is the parent's liquidity and the refinancing negotiation, which matter most and stay unobservable until a deal is signed.

The fitting precedent is not the economic cycle but leverage entering a development phase. Regional casinos have low cyclicality, with material declines only in 2008-09 and 2020. Every time the AlphaSense search looked, lease-adjusted leverage above about 7x on entering a development phase preceded a restructuring, and no operator closed a gap of this kind without an equity injection, a large asset sale or a restructuring. The sector's rule of thumb, "taxes, licences and bans move these share prices more than demand does", applies to Bally's on three fronts at once.

Strongest counter-case: the mechanics contain more flexibility than the headline suggests. The flexibility includes the 25% utilisation carve-out, two equity cures, a 3.5% payment-in-kind (PIK) toggle, $85m a year of non-cash interest, property-level rent coverage near 2x, a landlord with 19.4% of its income at stake, "multiple third parties interested" in Chicago, and gaming regulators that prefer capital infusions to revoking licences (New York with Empire Resorts; Rhode Island in 2020). All true, and all of it points to the survival of the operating company, which is not the same as the survival of the common equity at today's value.

What would change my view. Either of two events would: a signed amendment with disclosed terms below a 10% blended cost and maturities beyond 2029; or removal of the going-concern paragraph in the FY2026 10-K.

Market versus me: the market knows the headline risk but not the mechanics. The market knows about the going-concern note but not the covenant and liquidity mechanics behind it. Some of the mechanics it has missed are positive for the credit; the ones it has missed for the equity are negative.

Score: 2, set by the Rater. The operating lines are simple and trackable (four drivers, third-party data monthly), but the equity is a binary set by lenders, the landlord and the sponsor within six months: a going-concern note, a covenant waiver running only to the Q1 2027 certificate, minimum liquidity tests, a 30% restructuring branch and a range from -100% to +35%, with risks that are sudden, correlated and base-case rather than tail, and net debt to EBITDA 16.1x (99th percentile, the Universe's worst) turning any operating miss into a solvency event. The parent carries all of Ballys Intralot's risks through its 58% pledged stake plus its own going-concern position, so it sits at the anchors' floor, beside Ballys Intralot and well below AT&S; the Risks groups at 4 and 16 agree.

10#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is bottoming on a financing bridge rather than turning up on fundamentals, and the terms of a capital-structure event within six months, not operating delivery, will decide its next phase.

The dashboard reads "Turning/Inflecting"; I read "bottoming after capitulation, with a collapse branch still live". The dashboard's rule is mechanical: the price is above its moving averages, and the 200-day average has risen in most months.

ForThe evidence for bottoming is in the share price and the shareholder base. The shares fell 26% on the going-concern note to $8.44 and then recovered 60% to a level between that low and the sponsor's $15 bid. Six-month returns are flat, short interest has been near zero since early 2025, and 47% of the 2025 free float has rolled into the sponsor's vehicle.

AgainstThe evidence against a turn upward is that nothing in the fundamentals has turned. EBITDA after rent falls in FY2027, interest rises, consensus has further to cut, and the going-concern language is unchanged. The rally came on a 13% loan that worsens the arithmetic.

RiskThe collapse phase is still on the table. A restructuring branch carries 30% probability, the unsecured notes at 63% to 70% of par are pricing a haircut, and the landlord's comfort is that it can replace the tenant.

The staircase ahead: the adverse steps are dated and near, while the favourable steps are binary and mostly later. A "thesis broadening" phase would require the Chicago casino's receipts to beat expectations and the refinancing to be clean; a "reinforcing" phase would need both, plus the UK holding up. The probability of reaching either phase within 18 months is the 5% to 10% I give to a clean refinancing or a take-private. The calendar below sets out each step.

Strongest counter-case: stocks that survive a going-concern capitulation often re-rate violently. Las Vegas Sands and MGM averted filings in 2009 with equity raises and debt exchanges and became the decade's best performers. If Standard General and GLPI together engineer Bally's survival, the phase could jump straight from bottoming to reinforcing. The precedents cut both ways, however: Sands and MGM raised public equity at the bottom, while Station Casinos and Caesars' operating company did not, and their public equity was extinguished.

What would change my view. The terms of the refinancing, in the first week they are public.

Score: 17, set by the Rater. The dashboard's Turning/Inflecting reads a 60% relief rally from the USD 8.44 capitulation on a 13% bridge loan; the memo's Bottoming is right about the price, but the fundamentals are still turning down together (EBITDA after rent falls in FY2027, interest rises, consensus has further to fall, the subsidiary's guidance is likely rebased, the going-concern language is unchanged) and a 30% collapse branch is live, with the dated next steps mostly negative. That is Bottoming in the price inside a Collapsing fundamental phase, so I place it just below Ballys Intralot's Collapsing and above Wizz Air, whose collapse is complete across every measure.

11#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the fair multiple is a trough enterprise-value multiple of 6x to 7x on the parent plus the subsidiary stake at a discount, which leaves the common equity with a fundamental value near zero and a market price made of sponsor and Chicago option value.

Viewforth's guideline cannot set a fair multiple for Bally's. Bally's has no multiple history, and its two-year-forward P/E of -1.4x is meaningless. The dashboard's starting phase, Turning/Inflecting, would ordinarily argue for the lower end of a historical range, but there is no range, because Bally's has reported no positive EPS since FY2019 and none is forecast.

My view: Bally's is not a P/E case and should not be forced into one. Four EPS bases exist, and the brokers' FY2027 EPS figures span -$2.87 to -$6.79 on the same EBITDA. Minorities, penny warrants, non-cash interest accretion and a share count that depends on the capital-structure branch make the per-share unit unreliable. The fair valuation is therefore a sum of the parts on enterprise value, with each claim's priority explicit.
ComponentBasisValue
Parent operating business after rentabout $100m to $120m of EBITDA a year, at 6x to 7x (Deutsche Bank 6.0x domestic; Jefferies 6.8x blended; Standard General's 2024 bid 7.8x forward; Caesars-Fertitta 7.5x)$0.6bn to $0.85bn
Chicago permanent casino, extra value$30m to $110m of EBITDA after rent at stabilisation, at 6x to 7x, less Bally's remaining spend of $0.4bn to $0.76bnabout zero (-$0.5bn to +$0.4bn)
Other options (Tropicana land, Star, the Bronx)highly uncertain; the Bronx carries $560m of 13% debt and a 2030 opening$0.2bn to $0.6bn

The consolidated EV/EBITDA of 14x is arithmetic, not a valuation. On FY2026 consensus, EV/EBITDA of 14x reflects a small equity sitting under a large, fixed enterprise value; it is not a multiple the market pays for Bally's earnings. The right comparison is the regional casino range of 6x to 8x, and on that range the common equity is a residual with little or no fundamental value.

The $13.52 price is about $8 to $13 a share of option premium above the sum of the parts. The premium has two sources: the sponsor option (with reference prices of $15 and $18.25) and the Chicago option (valued at management's $250m rather than our $150m). A fair "multiple" for this phase is therefore a probability-weighted option value, not a cash-flow multiple: a survival-with-dilution case supports $5 to $8 a share, a restructuring $0 to $2, a take-private $15 to $18, and a clean refinancing with a strong Chicago opening $20 or more.

No peer offers an anchor for a P/E comparison. Every listed peer carries far less leverage than Bally's 18x lease-inclusive net debt to EBITDA, and Bally's Intralot's 29.9x P/E reflects depressed earnings.

Strongest counter-case: in a controlled company, the controller sets the price. Sum-of-the-parts analyses of controlled companies are routinely wrong for that reason: Standard General paid 7.8x forward EV/EBITDA in 2024, and $18.25 a share in 2025 after an activist pushed it up from $15. If the next event is a bid, the "fair multiple" is whatever the board's special committee extracts. That is why the sponsor option is worth something, and I weight it at 5%.

What would change my view. A refinancing below 10% would raise the parent's multiple from the trough 6x to 7x toward 8x and add about $0.2bn to equity value; the Chicago casino at $250m of stabilised EBITDAR would add about $0.6bn.

Score: 10, set by the Rater. Measure 1 cannot be read; on the memo's peer comparison the stock is far more than 15% dearer than peers, which gives at least D, and step 2 moves it to F because a business in a collapsing fundamental phase with a going-concern note deserves a lower multiple than its peers, not a higher one, and the memo's fair value for the common is near zero to USD 5 against USD 13.52. I place it at the middle of F rather than the floor because part of the premium is a genuine sponsor and Chicago option (bid references at USD 15 and 18.25) rather than pure mispricing.

12#12 Total shareholder return (DuPont framework)

Conclusion: the expected 18-month return is about -40% on a bimodal distribution, driven by the capital-structure branch rather than by earnings, with a 5% to 10% tail of +50% or more that depends on the sponsor and on Chicago.

The model's standard return calculation cannot be used for Bally's. At a guideline fair multiple of 0.0x on negative two-year-forward earnings, the model computes a return of -1,607% to 31 December 2027 and -1,567% to 30 June 2029, and its split (-365% from the multiple, +468% from earnings on the template's trailing basis) has no meaning. This memo therefore gives the return on an enterprise-value basis and by capital-structure branch, which is how the co-movement data say the market values the shares.

The DuPont decomposition on the model's base case (the debt-bridge branch), with EBITDA after rent in place of earnings, shows that the change in net debt decides the return:

0
Earnings growth: none. EBITDA after rent moves from $483m (FY2026) to $486m (FY2028), and EPS moves from -$6.28 to a more negative -$8.91. The earnings component contributes nothing positive over either horizon.
0 or less
Change in the multiple: zero or negative. The consolidated EV/EBITDA of 14x is arithmetic, not a valuation, and at a fair trough multiple of 6x to 7x the equity is negative, so no re-rating to a fair multiple helps the common equity.
none
Dividends and cash returns: none. None is plausible before FY2030, because Rhode Island's terms block payments to the parent above 5.5x leverage and the credit agreement blocks restricted payments above 4.25x.
-$1.2bn
The item DuPont omits, which decides this case: the change in net debt at a constant enterprise value. On the model, net debt rises $0.66bn in FY2027 and $0.53bn in FY2028. At a constant enterprise value, that rise transfers $1.2bn from equity holders to lenders over the period, more than today's market capitalisation. On its own base case, the model's equity value goes to zero unless enterprise value rises by more than $1.2bn, which needs the Chicago casino well above $150m of EBITDAR or a multiple expansion at the parent that the lifecycle phase does not justify.

My probability-weighted value over 18 months (to mid-2028) is about $8 a share, 40% below the price:

BranchWeightValue per shareContribution
Debt bridge or amend-and-extend40%$8 to $14 (survival; the equity's claim shrinking)$4.4
Sponsor-led recapitalisation (third-party capital, senior or dilutive)20%$5 to $8$1.3
Restructuring (distressed exchange, debt-for-equity swap, Chapter 11)30%$0 to $2$0.3
Take-private5%$15 to $18$0.8
Clean refinancing below 10% blended, Chicago on time5%$20 to $25$1.1
Expected valueabout $8; -40% against $13.52

Over three years (to mid-2029), the survival branches widen in both directions, and the expected value stays similar with fatter tails. With the Chicago casino stabilised at $150m and UK online at a 30% margin, FY2029 EBITDA is about $549m against net debt of about $7.2bn, so the equity remains thin unless the market pays a multiple above 13x. The bull case (Chicago at $250m, interest refinanced below 10%, Evoke synergies at the subsidiary) could support $20 to $30 a share. The restructuring branch stays near zero. The three-year expected value is similar to the 18-month figure, with fatter tails, because the 2029 springing maturity and Evoke's 2028 refinancing add a second decision point.

Four drivers set the return, in order of importance.

(1) The capital-structure branch: it decides whether the equity has a claim at all.
→
(2) The Chicago casino's first two quarters of Illinois Gaming Board receipts: the only driver that can lift enterprise value enough to offset the debt build.
→
(3) The refinancing price: each 300bp is about $90m a year, which at 6.5x is $0.6bn of enterprise value.
→
(4) UK and core casino demand: small.

Strongest counter-case: the equity is an option, and options like this one have paid before. Options on a thin free float with a motivated controlling holder have paid out: the 2024 to 2025 take-private process delivered $18.25 to holders who bought at $10 to $12. A 5% weight on a take-private may be too low if Standard General's cheapest route to a solution is to own 100% and recapitalise privately with a partner. I would raise that weight to 10% if the permanent CFO comes from a sponsor-finance background.

What would change my view. Any of the dated events in the #10 calendar turning out positive would: liquidity comfortably above $325m with the revolver less than 25% drawn; Bally's Intralot keeping €422m with UK growth above 6%; an extension of the Chicago deadline granted on 10 December without damages; or refinancing terms below 10%.

Market versus me: the share price is more optimistic than the brokers' own targets. The mean target price of $10.50 (-22%) is close to my expected value. The share price embeds a sponsor premium that the sell-side will not model.

Score: 5, set by the Rater. A loss of about 40% gives F and maps below the -30% point (about 5) on the scale; there is no earnings growth, no multiple support and no dividend, and the net debt build of USD 1.2bn transfers more than today's market capitalisation from equity to lenders at constant EV. The 5% to 10% tail of +50% or more (take-private or clean refinancing) does not offset a 30% restructuring branch worth USD 0 to 2, so the skew holds it at the floor area of the band.

13#13 Summary conclusion

Bally's is a case Richard should understand and, at this price, leave to the credit investors and the landlord. The operating business is fine: a stable regional casino estate with property-level rent coverage near 2x, a UK online business that mitigates the duty better than any other in the sector, a US online unit that has reached breakeven, and a flagship Chicago casino that will open in 2027.

None of that operating strength reaches the common equity. Rent plus interest exceed EBITDAR from FY2027. The parent needs $300m to $400m of new money a year even after the Chicago casino stabilises. The best assets sit in a 58%-owned, ring-fenced subsidiary whose market value exceeds the parent's market capitalisation. The sponsor who will design the solution has $647m of its own capital and a record of using other people's capital on its own terms.

The forecasts are more predictable than usual above the fixed-charge line and less predictable than almost any peer's below it. Consensus is still 15% too high on FY2027 EBITDA and $118m too low on interest. The next six months (Q3 liquidity, Bally's Intralot on 27 November, the Chicago deadline on 10 December and the refinancing by March 2027) will decide the capital-structure branch.

The configuration Richard looks for is absent; its mirror image is present. Richard looks for positively skewed outcomes with the probability of upgrades on his side. Bally's offers a predictable operating base under an unpredictable, downward-skewed equity claim, and that configuration is clearly visible now.

What would turn the case. A refinancing below 10% that removes the going-concern doubt, followed by Chicago casino receipts above $30m a month, would make Bally's a "Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU" setup, with consensus too low on Chicago and too high on interest. That combination has a 5% to 10% probability, and the calendar in #10 names the events that would reveal it. Until then, the better ways to own the parts that work are Bally's Intralot (UK consolidation, lottery contracts and Evoke synergies, at 5.8x net debt to EBITDA) and GLPI (the Chicago real estate at an 8.5% yield, with the backstop of a replacement tenant).

Ratings

FThesis's Change Forces' Strength

The forces of change are strong, dated and almost all negative for the common equity (fixed charges, fiscal policy, Chicago politics and a sponsor-led recapitalisation); the positive forces accrue to the subsidiary and the landlord.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 9, set by the Rater. Both input forces are strongly negative (external 21: the UK duty, Chicago terminals and the price of credit; internal 10: a sponsor-led, value-transferring capital event, a hollowed finance function) and the financial output confirms it (topic 6 F, 5: losses widen to about -USD 8.8 a share and stay there), so the net change is strong, dated and reaches profits surely, in the wrong direction. The positives (Chicago, UK consolidation, US online at breakeven) accrue mainly to the subsidiary and the landlord, which is the 10 level: strong negative change on both sides with profits falling.

FFoundations' Robustness

Bally's is a going-concern company with negative returns on capital, the sector's highest leverage, an unclean earnings base, material weaknesses in controls and a hollowed-out finance function; the moats it has are owned 58% or restricted.

Foundations' Robustness: 11, set by the Rater. Quality of the business is 13 and the delivery record 9, and they compound: a sound, low-cyclical industry and a stable regional estate with property-level rent coverage near 2x are real, but they protect the landlord and the credit, while the common rests on the sector's worst financial profile (negative ROIC, 16x leverage, negative free cash flow, a going-concern note), moats that are owned 58% or restricted, governance run for the controller and a record of cuts and abandonment. Unlike CVS Group, the operating stability does not make the business robust because the capital structure consumes all of it, so this is the 10 level, held just above it by Rhode Island and the estate's stability.

FSetups' Fit/Crispness

None of the six Target Setups fits: Bally's is not a quality business, its cause for concern is solvency rather than a clearing event, and its corporate change transfers value rather than raising earnings power. The nearest fit, "Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU", would apply only after a clean refinancing and a strong Chicago opening.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 6, set by the Rater. The memo finds no Target Setup fits and calls the case the mirror image of one: not a quality business, a cause for concern that is solvency rather than a clearing event, and corporate change that transfers value rather than raising earnings power. The nearest, Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU, needs a clean refinancing and a strong Chicago opening that are 5% to 10% likely, and today's going-concern problem contradicts its mechanism outright, so this is the 10 level, at its lower end.

FCase Riskiness

The equity outcome is binary and set by counterparties within six months, with correlated, high-magnitude risks that are part of the base case rather than the tail, and the per-share unit itself is unreliable.

Case Riskiness: 3, set by the Rater. Riskiness and simplicity is at 2 and nothing here lifts it: the operating case is simple and trackable, but the equity outcome is a binary set by counterparties within six months, with correlated, base-case solvency risks, an unreliable per-share unit and leverage that has already turned the balance sheet into the problem. That is the 10 level and below, a binary and opaque case where a miss means restructuring rather than a de-rating.

Basis of the figures. "EBITDA" is the company's Adjusted EBITDA after rent paid to GLPI, which is the brokers' basis; "EBITDAR" is EBITDA before rent. Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 1, whose base case is the debt-funded bridge. Q3 2026 results are due within days of the memo date and are not in the files; Bally's Intralot reports on 27 November 2026.

Forecast inputs. I change no forecast input and write no inputs-changed.md. I keep every input of the second set of forecast inputs unchanged, for three reasons. The base case already carries the lean the record justifies (Chicago a quarter late at 60% of the analysts' stabilised earnings, core casinos flat, UK online below consensus, interest well above consensus). The third set's reconciliation found no input wrong. And my own differences lie in the branch weights (debt bridge 40%, recapitalisation 20%, restructuring 30%, take-private 5%, clean refinancing 5%), which are not model inputs. Two points for the Financial Analyst stand from the third set: the model's H1 2026 EBITDA actuals should be on the company's Adjusted EBITDA basis, so that H2 2026 is not force-fitted, and the 60.6m share count should apply to the whole of FY2026.

Points to reconcile. The memo cites minimum liquidity of $325m (insight 6, the #10 calendar and #12) and of $300m for Q4 2026 (the #9 table), and revolver commitments of about $319m after the October step-down alongside a reported $460m extension to October 2028. The Q3 2026 10-Q should settle both.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

Minority interests are material: 179.0% of market capitalisation. Our earnings per share are before them; consensus earnings per share are after them.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
